title: Dead Letter Queues
description: Learn how dead letter queues handle poison messages, implement retry strategies with exponential backoff, and set up monitoring that catches problems before they cascade.

segments.text: A poison message is one that can never be successfully processed. Maybe it has malformed JSON, references a deleted user, or triggers a bug in your consumer code. Without a DLQ, this message blocks the queue forever — other messages pile up behind it.

Before sending to the DLQ, retry with exponential backoff. First retry after one second, then two, then four, then eight. Cap at a maximum — say sixty seconds. This handles transient failures like database connection blips. Typically three to five retries before declaring a message dead.

Always add jitter to your backoff. Without jitter, if a downstream service goes down and comes back, all retrying consumers hit it simultaneously — the thundering herd problem. AWS recommends full jitter: random delay between zero and the backoff interval. This spreads retries evenly.

SQS has native DLQ support. You set a maxReceiveCount on the source queue — say five. After five failed processing attempts, SQS automatically moves the message to the designated DLQ. The message retains all its attributes plus a receive count for debugging.

Kafka doesn't have native DLQs. Instead, you create error topics. When a consumer can't process a message from orders-events, it publishes to orders-events-dlq topic. You need to build this yourself. The advantage is Kafka retains the full message with its offset, so you can trace exactly what happened.
A message lands in the DLQ. Now what? In many teams, DLQ messages just rot there forever. Think about what a proper DLQ handling workflow should look like.
segments.thought_prompt: What should happen after a message lands in the DLQ? How do you prevent messages from being silently lost?

segments.text: DLQ replay is critical. Fix the bug that caused the failure, then replay messages from the DLQ back to the original queue. SQS supports DLQ redrive natively. For Kafka, you build a replay consumer that reads from the error topic and republishes to the source topic. Always replay to staging first.

DLQ monitoring saves you. Alert when the DLQ depth exceeds a threshold — say one hundred messages in ten minutes. At Uber, DLQ alerts are treated as SEV-2 incidents because each dead message represents a failed business operation — a ride not matched, a payment not processed.

Classify DLQ messages. Transient failures — retry later. Permanent failures — bad data, needs manual fix. Bug-caused failures — fix code, then replay. Each category has a different handling path. Without classification, your on-call engineer wastes hours triaging every DLQ alert.

Consider this real scenario. Your payment processing DLQ has fifty thousand messages from a three-hour outage. You've fixed the bug. But replaying all fifty thousand simultaneously will overwhelm the payment service. What's your approach?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you safely replay 50,000 DLQ messages without overwhelming downstream services?

segments.text: Dead letter queues are your safety net for message processing. The key practices: exponential backoff with jitter before DLQ, classify failures by type, alert on DLQ depth with clear thresholds, build replay tooling before you need it, and always test replay in staging. A DLQ without monitoring is just a graveyard for lost data.
